tagline: Forest gravel winds through hardwood hills past a CCC lookout tower.
intro: Sugar Camp combines 20 miles of paved highway with eight miles of maintained gravel on a 28-mile drive. The Forest Service presents this National Forest Scenic Byway as a winding route through wooded hills and valleys, with vistas of distant landscapes. Mixed hardwoods share the hills with eastern red cedar and pine. Farms and pastures also belong to the route, while the gravel stretch carries travelers farther into the woods with each turn. Onyx and Sugar Camp Tower provide places to stop and picnic.
Settlers tapped sugar maples here for sap. Another chapter of forest work left a more conspicuous structure: the Civilian Conservation Corps built Sugar Camp Fire Tower in the 1930s.

From Highway 112 south of Roaring River State Park, the route turns onto Forest Road 197. Forest Road 1004 leads to the tower; Onyx Observation Area follows about 1.5 miles later. The gravel reaches Highway 86 near Table Rock Lake, and the remaining drive winds through forest toward the Cassville area. Highway 86 continues to the forest boundary just south of Bates Corner, where it meets Highway 76.

moments.title: Roaring River State Park
moments.text: A medicine-show fortune helped create Roaring River State Park. Thomas Mark “Doc” Sayman bought 2,400 acres and gave them to the state after failing to persuade the game and fish commission to purchase the spring property. The park was acquired in 1923, then developed by the Civilian Conservation Corps and Works Progress Administration between 1933 and 1939. The CCC rebuilt an earlier mill dam for the fish hatchery in 1933. Its Deer Leap Trail has rough stone steps, retaining walls and an overlook. The rustic stone bath house survives from a CCC lake-and-beach project that was never completed.

moments.title: Sugar Camp Lookout Tower
moments.text: Sugar Camp’s fire tower dates from the Civilian Conservation Corps’ work in the 1930s. It stands off Forest Road 1004, reached shortly after joining Forest Road 197. The tower site provides a picnic stop, with one table. Climbing the tower is prohibited.

moments.title: Onyx Observation Area
moments.text: Onyx is a roadside pull-off with a view of the Ozark Highlands. It follows the Sugar Camp tower turn about 1.5 miles along the drive. Two picnic tables and parking for two vehicles make this a small stopping place on the forest route. The gravel road eventually meets Highway 86 near Table Rock Lake.
moments.notice: The Onyx pull-off looks across the Ozark Highlands.
